Appendix A
Supplied Field Questionnaire and Scoring
Key
The following reproduces the content of the supplied bilingual F1.0 form,
with layout adapted for the thesis. The Markdown and HTML versions are archived
under survey_instruments. They document the instrument supplied for this study;
no independent translation-validation result is inferred. The wider platform's pre-
broadcast, echo-triggered, and weekly instrument proposals are not presented as
questions administered in this eld wave.
A.1
Information and Consent Wording
Title: LOKLOK Media Listening & Trust Questionnaire (F1.0).
Researcher: Sherif Rashwan  LOKLOK social-media radio network re-
search. Purpose: Understand how university students evaluate broadcast quality,
source trust, and content diversity while listening during a car / Uber ride.
Consent: Anonymous, voluntary, academic use only. No right/wrong an-
swers; skip any item. Duration approximately 5 min. Condentiality: No identi-
fying data; reported only in aggregate. The supplied form uses English explanatory
prose with bilingual labels. These statements are reproduced as instrument wording,

A.2
Section 0: About You
1. Age: open numerical response.
2. Gender: male; female.
3. Academic year: rst, second, third, or fourth.
4. Faculty: Mass Communication; Commerce; Engineering; Science; Other, spec-
ify.
5. University: select one of the following source-form categories:
 October 6 University (O6U).
 Cairo University  6th of October Branch.
 Misr University for Science & Technology (MUST).
 Modern University for Technology & Information (MTI).
 Sadat Academy for Management Sciences  6th of October.
 Higher Institutes of 6th of October City.
 Other: specify.
The form explicitly excludes Ahram Canadian University (ACU). Institution
names are source-form labels, not independent verication of campus geogra-
phy or ocial institutional nomenclature.
6. Listening context: Uber; private car; microbus; public transport.

APPENDIX A. SUPPLIED FIELD QUESTIONNAIRE AND SCORING KEY
252
A.3
Section A: Judging a Radio Broadcaster
Think of a broadcaster/program you listened to during the ride. Rate 04: 0 =
strongly disagree; 1 = disagree; 2 = neutral; 3 = agree; 4 = strongly agree.
BR1
The broadcaster veries claims before going on air
BR2
The broadcaster corrects mistakes quickly and openly
BR3
The broadcaster stays fair when opinions clash
BR4
The broadcaster exaggerates to gain attention
SV1
Students whose opinion I respect follow and like this broadcaster
SV2
Interacting with the audience shows the broadcaster cares
SV3
A high social rating makes me trust the broadcaster more
SV4
The broadcaster's popularity is a sign of its credibility
IQ1 The content I heard is well-informed and substantial

APPENDIX A. SUPPLIED FIELD QUESTIONNAIRE AND SCORING KEY
253
IQ2 The broadcaster adds value beyond what I already know
IQ3 The program content is consistently high quality
A.4
Section B: The Broadcast Experience
After listening, rate 17, from strongly disagree to strongly agree.
PB1
I feel more condent about what I heard after listening
PB2
The content exposed me to diverse perspectives I hadn't considered
PB3
I trust this broadcaster more than others on similar topics
PB4
The broadcast structure helped me understand the topic clearly
PB5
Overall, the broadcast was of high quality and worth my time
A.5
Section C: Overall Rating
How would you rate this broadcast? Select 15: 1 = poor; 5 = excellent.

APPENDIX A. SUPPLIED FIELD QUESTIONNAIRE AND SCORING KEY
254
A.6
Scoring and Analysis Boundaries
Reverse BR4 as 4 −BR4. BR, SV, and IQ are means of four, four, and three items
respectively; the broadcaster-battery total used for alpha contains all 11 scored
items. PB is the arithmetic mean of PB1PB5 on its original 17 scale. The star
response remains a separate 15 variable. No missing item cells occur in the supplied
60 questionnaires, so the recheck does not impute values or exercise a missing-item
prorating rule.
The 04 and 17 anchors must not be interchanged. PB3 measures compara-
tive trust, not intention to verify; PB4 measures structural clarity, not the inuence
of a displayed BRS. SV3 directly concerns a high social rating, but even this item
records perceived inuence rather than an experimentally identied badge eect.
The HTML/Markdown form, scored CSV, and qualitative notes are dierent arti-
facts; ride mood and recorded quotations do not become additional questionnaire
scale items simply because they can be linked.
